agency-reduces-happiness: Being the one who decides makes participants less happy, whatever the outcome turns out to be.
alt-agency-aversion-not-guilt: Deciding on another person's behalf is unpleasant in itself, whether or not the partner comes to harm.
alt-guilt-effect-driven-by-own-outcome: The unhappiness after a partner's loss comes from the participant's own bad outcome, not from guilt about the partner.
alt-imaging-contrast-invalid: The imaging pipeline does not recover effects that are already established, so its condition differences mean nothing.
alt-model-based-glm-invalid: The model-based fMRI analysis does not recover known brain signals, so its partner reward-surprise regressors cannot be trusted.
alt-participants-insensitive-to-value: Participants chose inattentively or at random, so their choices carry no information about what they preferred or felt.
alt-social-context-shifts-risk-attitude: Choosing on someone else's behalf simply changes how much risk a person will accept, and that is what the differences reflect.
guilt-effect-independent-of-own-outcome: The drop in happiness after a partner's loss appears whether or not the participant won their own lottery.
guilt-reduces-happiness-after-partner-lo: Participants become less happy after a partner's bad outcome when they made the choice than when the partner did.
guilt-signature-no-individual-difference: How closely a participant's brain response matches the published guilt signature does not predict their behavioural guilt effect.
happiness-correlates-partner-reward: Participants' moment-to-moment happiness rises with their own winnings and also with their partner's.
hypothesis-insula-tracks-interpersonal-g: Anterior insula carries interpersonal guilt, responding when the participant's own choice is what harmed the partner.
hypothesis-responsibility-weights-partne: A partner's unexpectedly bad outcomes lower a participant's happiness in their own right when the participant's choice caused them.
hypothesis-sts-mentalizes-partner-state-: Superior temporal sulcus represents what the partner is feeling only when the participant is responsible for the partner's outcome.
insula-guilt-replicates-yu-koban-signatu: The anterior insula guilt response matches the published Yu and Koban brain signature of guilt.
insula-ifg-connectivity-guilt: Anterior insula and inferior frontal gyrus are more strongly coupled when the participant is the one choosing for the partner.
insula-tracks-guilt-effect: The anterior insula responds more when a partner loses because of the participant's choice.
interprets-yu-koban-guilt-signature: Yu and Koban derived a whole-brain activity pattern that identifies guilt across paradigms, weighted most heavily on anterior insula.
lottery-choice-increases-with-ev: Participants chose the lottery more often the more it was worth, in both studies.
partner-algorithm-deception-assumption: The partner was an expected-value-maximising algorithm rather than a person, and participants were never told so.
precuneus-tpj-mpfc-social-decisions: Precuneus, left temporoparietal junction and medial prefrontal cortex respond more when deciding for a partner than for oneself alone.
prediction-behavioral-guilt-effect: Happiness should fall further after a partner's bad outcome when the participant chose than when the partner chose.
prediction-insula-tracks-guilt: Anterior insula should respond more when the participant chose than when the partner chose, after partner losses but not partner wins.
prediction-responsibility-model-wins-com: A happiness model that gives its own weight to partner losses the participant caused should fit the ratings better than models without one.
prediction-sts-tracks-partner-rpe-under-: Left superior temporal sulcus should track partner reward surprises on participant-chosen trials but not on partner-chosen ones.
responsibility-modulates-guilt-computati: A happiness model with a responsibility term accounts for the guilt effect better than models without one.
risk-premiums-null-social-solo: Risk premiums were no different when participants chose for a partner than when they chose for themselves alone, in either study.
scope-two-study-design: All findings come from two studies, an fMRI study and a behavioural replication, using the same lottery task with an algorithmic partner.
social-prpe-weight-positive: Partner reward surprises that the participant's own choice produced carry their own weight in happiness, in both studies.
solo-vs-social-choice-difference: Participants took the lottery slightly more often when choosing for themselves alone in the first study, but not in the second.
sts-tracks-partner-reward-prediction-err: Superior temporal sulcus tracks surprises in the partner's reward only when the participant made the choice.
ventral-striatum-tracks-computational-re: Ventral striatum on both sides responds more the larger the reward the computational model expects.
ventral-striatum-tracks-risky-choices: Ventral striatum responds more when participants take the risky lottery rather than the safe option, whoever they are choosing for.
